newsitem.title: UK: Stockpiling hides world copper surplus - Bloomsbury.
newsitem.headline: Stockpiling hides world copper surplus - Bloomsbury.

text.p: The world is already substantially in a surplus of refined copper but this is obscured during phases of government stockpiling, said analyst Bloomsbury Minerals Economics Ltd.

In its latest copper briefing service Bloomsbury said the surplus became very clear during pauses in the stockpiling process, when all of the surplus showed up in the market sector (on the London Metal Exchange).

A study of 1996 data showed that world copper production exceeded consumption by 85,000 tonnes in the first three-quarters of the year. For the full year the global surplus could be put at 100,000 tonnes.

But at the same time the market sector was in deficit by around 50-100,000 tonnes because around 150-200,000 tonnes of copper was taken off the market and put into government stockpiles, Bloomsbury said.

The world surplus is going to worsen over the next three years as new projects come on stream and the smelter bottleneck eases, and cumulative stock increases could be 600,000 tonnes over the 1996-1999 period.

But the market is not likely to suffer from the full weight of the physical surplus given there is some truth in widespread talk that China has authorised the addition of several hundred thousand tonnes to its copper stockpile over its 1996-2000 five-year plan period.

If purchases from the London Metal Exchange remain the chosen method (for Chinese stockpliling), the overall effect could be to discourage speculative shorting of the market, making price support easier, Bloomsbury said.
